FOREWORD (to the Third Edition) THE Universal Decimal Classification (U.D.C.), originally oerived from the Devvey Decimal Classification (D.C.), has been, and is still being, extended for use in classifying artic1es in periodicals, monographs and documents of all kinds, under the auspices of the Federation Internationale de Documentation (F.I.D.), which authorizes publication of various international editions in different languages (see end flyleaf). The preparation of the full English edition, parts of which have been already published as B.S. 1000, was originally-undertaken by the British Standards Institution at the joint request of the British Society for International Bibliography (B.S.I.B.) and the Association of Special Libraries and Information Bureaux (A.S.L.I.B.), now amalgamated in Aslib. It is the fourth full international edition and has the approval of the Lake Placid Club Education Foundation, New York, the body responsible for the Dewey Decimal Classification. The abridged edition B.S. lOOOA was first published in 1948 ,in response to a widespread demand for a comprehensive short edition in English, suitable as an introduction to the use of the full schedules and as a manual for classifying books and general documents in libraries, for which the full schedules are unnecessarily detailed. It was based on the oflicial Dutch abridgment, fifth edition (1946), and owed much to the abridgment published in English by H.M. Stationery Office under the title "Classification for Works ill Pure and Applied Science in the Science Museum Library," third edition (1936). In the radically revised second edition of 1957, account was taken of amendments internationally approved and authorized by the F.LD. up to 1955, and the tables corre- sponded closely to the English text of the Trilingual Abridged Edition B.S. loo0B: 1958, the international standard abridged edition of the UD.C. The alphabetical index contained over 20,000 entries, as against 2,000 in the first edition, while the terminology was revised throughout. Members of the British U.D.C. Committee, together with interested specialists too numerous to mention, gave freely of their expert advice and criticism, and the ;British Standards Institution takes this opportunity of expressing its indebtedness to them and also to the many users all over the world who have made suggestions for improving the schedules and the terminology.
